title: UK aviation emissions to be 50% higher than thought by 2050, government admits - Carbon Brief
gist: Quietly published UK government forecasts (June 2026) cut projected gains from sustainable aviation fuels, battery planes and fuel-efficiency tech, pushing projected 2050 aviation emissions to 28.1MtCO2e — about 9MtCO2e (50%) above the 'jet-zero' strategy's 19.3MtCO2e target — undermining the tech-based justification for a third Heathrow runway and shifting the burden onto costly carbon removal or afforestation.

insights.claim: The UK government's June 2026 'technology development' forecast projects UK aviation emissions of 28.1MtCO2e in 2050, versus the earlier 'jet-zero' strategy's target of 19.3MtCO2e — an increase of roughly 9MtCO2e, or about 50%.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A formal, government-acknowledged emissions gap of this size implies the UK will need much larger volumes of carbon dioxide removal or land-use offsets to hit its 2050 net-zero target — a durable policy and offset-market signal, not noise.
insights.quote: Its “technology development” pathway, with “ambitious carbon abatement measures”, only sees emissions drop to 28.1MtCO2e in 2050.

insights.claim: The government now expects sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) to make up only 30% of UK aviation fuel by 2050, down from a prior 50% assumption, and concedes SAFs will save less carbon over their lifecycle than previously modeled.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A government-level downgrade of SAF uptake and lifecycle carbon savings reduces the credibility of demand projections SAF producers and investors may be relying on for the UK market.
insights.quote: The government now expects SAFs to make up 30% of aviation fuel by 2050, rather than 50%.

insights.claim: New analysis from the Aviation Impact Accelerator, commissioned by the UK government, produced 'less optimistic' fuel-efficiency projections than earlier work, cutting the assumed annual aircraft fuel-efficiency improvement rate from 2% per year (jet-zero strategy) to 1.3% per year in the new scenario.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A roughly one-third cut to the assumed efficiency-improvement rate implies airlines' per-flight emissions will fall more slowly than modeled, a headwind for any investment thesis built on rapid organic decarbonisation of existing fleets.
insights.quote: Fuel-efficiency improvements have therefore been revised downward from 2% per year in the “jet-zero” strategy to 1.3% in the new “technology development” scenario.
insights.locator: For its new forecasts, the government commissioned

insights.claim: The new UK forecast assumes a reduced role for battery-powered aircraft, with only some of the smallest zero-emissions aircraft expected to be in commercial use by 2035.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Tempers the near-term UK commercial case for electric-aviation technology developers targeting mid-2030s entry into service.
insights.locator: There is also a reduced role for battery-powered planes

insights.claim: The roughly 50% upward revision in projected 2050 UK aviation emissions is driven jointly by lower expected SAF uptake, weaker fuel-efficiency gains, a smaller role for battery-powered aircraft, and lower assumed international carbon prices — a multi-factor downgrade rather than a single technology disappointment.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A broad-based, multi-technology downgrade signals a structural gap between clean-aviation technology promises and delivery, not a one-off forecasting error — relevant to any thesis premised on aviation tech solving emissions on schedule.
insights.quote: The shift is down to much lower expectations for SAF uptake, fuel-efficiency improvements and the roll-out of battery-powered planes, as well as lower international carbon prices.
insights.locator: The shift is down to much lower expectations

insights.claim: Even the UK's more modest goal of 22% SAF uptake by 2040 would require enormous, potentially unattainable, volumes of waste products — currently the main SAF feedstock source.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Flags a physical feedstock-supply bottleneck for SAF-dependent decarbonisation plans, a risk factor for airlines and SAF producers counting on waste-based feedstock scaling.
insights.quote: Even meeting the UK’s relatively modest goal of 22% SAF uptake by 2040 would require enormous – potentially unattainable – volumes of waste products, which are currently the main source of the fuel.

insights.claim: Under a 'current trends' no-new-policy scenario — flight numbers rising without new decarbonisation policy or innovation — UK aviation emissions would reach 41.1MtCO2e by 2050, roughly double the level targeted by the jet-zero strategy and recommended by the Climate Change Committee (CCC).
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Defines the policy-risk ceiling investors should track: failure to implement new decarbonisation policy roughly doubles the emissions overshoot versus the CCC-recommended path, raising odds of future demand-management measures (e.g., flight taxes, growth caps).
insights.quote: in which emissions increase to 41.1MtCO2e by 2050

insights.claim: The government's new forecasts assume UK airport passenger numbers will be at least 50% higher by 2050, including planned Heathrow expansion, which runs counter to Climate Change Committee (CCC) advice that passenger-number growth may need to be limited to keep aviation emissions down.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Highlights an explicit policy tension between a growth-oriented UK aviation strategy and its own climate advisors' recommendations — a recurring source of legal/political challenge risk to airport-expansion projects.
insights.quote: Overall, passenger numbers would be at least 50% higher by 2050.

themes.theme: Heathrow third runway and carbon-budget fallout

insights.claim: Aviation Environment Federation (AEF) calculations based on government data suggest Heathrow's proposed third runway would add a relatively modest 3.5MtCO2e per year of emissions by 2050, but with emissions from the runway expected to keep rising significantly beyond the 2050 net-zero deadline.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Quantifies a specific, attributable emissions liability tied to the Heathrow third-runway decision that policymakers and challengers can cite directly in the 2029 planning decision.
insights.locator: AEF calculations, based on government data

insights.claim: Tim Johnson, director of the Aviation Environment Federation, argues that reduced reliance on clean-aviation technology 'reopens the debate' about the scale of greenhouse gas removals needed and how to manage the projected 50% growth in air-travel demand, framing the government's revised forecast as more honest but also more exposed on the removals question.
insights.speaker: Tim Johnson, director, Aviation Environment Federation
insights.so_what: A credible industry-adjacent voice shifting the framing from 'technology solves it' to 'removals must compensate' signals where future UK aviation-climate policy debate and lobbying will concentrate.
insights.quote: Less reliance on cleaner technology and fuels reopens the debate about the role and scale of greenhouse gas removals and ways to tackle the projected 50% growth in demand for air travel.
insights.locator: Tim Johnson, director at the Aviation Environment Federation

insights.claim: Dr Lois Pennington, a University of Manchester research associate who has studied Heathrow's emissions impact, says the new government forecast shows the UK is already projected to exceed aviation's fair share of the carbon budget even before a third runway at Heathrow is factored in, meaning any approval would knowingly breach legally binding carbon budgets.
insights.speaker: Dr Lois Pennington, University of Manchester
insights.so_what: An academic on-record framing turns Heathrow approval into a knowing breach of legal carbon budgets rather than a forecasting uncertainty — raises legal-challenge risk for the 2029 planning decision.
insights.quote: For Heathrow, it means expansion can no longer be waved through on the promise of technology, and any approvals will be in the full knowledge that it will bust our legally binding carbon budgets.
insights.locator: Dr Lois Pennington, a research associate

insights.claim: With clean-aviation technology now expected to deliver smaller emissions cuts, closing the gap to the UK's 2050 net-zero target for aviation would require either large-scale new forest planting or reliance on carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies that the article describes as costly and largely unproven.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Shifts the practical offset burden for UK aviation's residual emissions onto CDR and land-use sectors that are themselves early-stage and expensive — a demand signal for CDR project developers and forestry/land investors, with execution risk attached.
insights.quote: these higher emissions from flights in 2050 would need to be taken out of the atmosphere using costly and largely unproven “carbon dioxide removal” technologies – or by planting gigantic new forests
insights.locator: If this is to be compatible with UK climate goals
